lesson.title: Three Digits That Tell the Whole Story
lesson.summary: Every HTTP response opens with a three digit status code whose first digit sorts it into one of five categories, informational, success, redirection, client error, or server error, letting software react correctly without parsing English text.
lesson.body:
The response line shown back in the HTTP protocol chapter, HTTP/1.1 200 OK, carries a status code, and that code is doing real work. The first digit sorts every possible outcome into one of five broad categories, and the remaining two digits narrow it down to something specific. A client can check just the first digit and already know roughly what happened, even for a status code it has never seen before.

1xx codes are informational and fairly rare in everyday browsing. 100 Continue, for example, lets a server tell a client that has announced it wants to send a large request body that it is fine to go ahead and send it, before the client commits the bandwidth.

2xx codes mean success. 200 OK is the general purpose everything worked response, the one shown for the GET request in the protocol chapter. 201 Created is returned after a POST that successfully made a new resource. 204 No Content signals success with nothing to send back in the body, which fits a DELETE that removed a resource cleanly and has nothing left to describe.

3xx codes mean redirection, and two of them are easy to confuse but mean different things. 301 Moved Permanently tells the client this resource now lives at a new URL for good, and well behaved clients should update any stored link and use the new location from now on. 302 Found means the same resource is temporarily at a different URL right now, and the client should keep using the original URL for future requests. 304 Not Modified is different again: it is returned when a client says, using conditional request headers, I already have a cached copy, has it changed, and the server confirms it has not, letting the client keep using what it already has without re downloading it.

4xx codes mean the problem is on the client's side. 400 Bad Request covers malformed syntax the server could not even parse. 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid credentials. 403 Forbidden means the credentials were fine but the client still is not allowed to do this. 404 Not Found means the resource simply does not exist at that URL. 405 Method Not Allowed means the resource exists but does not support the method that was used on it. 429 Too Many Requests means the client has been rate limited and should slow down.

5xx codes mean the problem is on the server's side, and retrying the exact same request unmodified might well succeed later. 500 Internal Server Error is the generic catch all for something going wrong while handling the request. 502 Bad Gateway means a server acting as a proxy or gateway got an invalid response from the server it was talking to upstream. 503 Service Unavailable means the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, often due to overload or maintenance.

Strung together, a realistic sequence might look like this: a client submits a login form with the wrong password and gets back 401 Unauthorized; they correct the password and resubmit, getting 200 OK along with a session; they then request a page that has since moved and get 301 Moved Permanently pointing at its new URL. Three requests, three different first digits, three different and entirely correct client reactions.
